questions.enonce_markdown:
State and explain five measures a country can use to correct a balance of payments deficit.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A **balance of payments deficit** exists when a country's **payments to the rest of the world are greater than its receipts**, that is when it spends more foreign exchange than it earns. The measures below increase receipts (exports) or reduce payments (imports).

**1. Export promotion.** The government gives **subsidies, tax relief, cheap credit and export guarantees**, organises trade fairs and improves ports and roads so that firms export more (for example cocoa, coffee, timber and bananas). More exports bring in **more foreign exchange** and reduce the deficit.

**2. Import restrictions (tariffs and quotas).** **Tariffs** (taxes on imports) and **quotas** (limits on quantities) raise the price or reduce the quantity of imports, so **spending on imports falls**. Their disadvantages are possible retaliation and higher prices for consumers.

**3. Import substitution.** The country **produces at home goods that it used to import** (for example rice, sugar, soap) by encouraging local industries. Imports fall and local jobs are created.

**4. Devaluation or depreciation of the currency.** Lowering the value of the currency makes **exports cheaper to foreigners and imports dearer** at home, so exports rise and imports fall, if demand for them is elastic. (This applies to a country that controls its own exchange rate; a currency tied to another one cannot easily use this tool.)

**5. Deflationary policies.** The government **reduces total spending** through higher taxes, lower government spending and higher interest rates. Incomes and prices fall, so people buy **fewer imports**, and domestic goods become cheaper to export.

**Other measures:** **exchange controls** (rationing foreign exchange), attracting **foreign investment and tourism**, and **borrowing or foreign aid** (a temporary solution).

**Conclusion.** A country can correct its deficit by raising exports and reducing imports, and the measures chosen depend on its economic situation.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define:

(i) Comparative cost advantage. (2 marks)

(ii) Absolute advantage. (2 marks)

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Comparative cost advantage (2 marks)**

A country has a **comparative (cost) advantage** in a good when it can produce it at a **lower opportunity cost** than another country, that is it **gives up fewer units of other goods** to produce one unit of it. Countries gain by specialising in the goods in which they have a comparative advantage and trading, even when one of them is better at producing everything.

**(ii) Absolute advantage (2 marks)**

A country has an **absolute advantage** in a good when it can produce it **using fewer resources per unit** (at a lower real cost), or **produce more of it with the same resources**, than another country.

*Difference:* absolute advantage compares the **quantities of resources used**, while comparative advantage compares the **opportunity costs**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain three methods of trade restrictions.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** **Trade restrictions** are measures by which a government limits imports (and sometimes exports) in order to protect local industries or the balance of payments.

**1. Tariffs (import duties).** A tariff is a **tax on imported goods**. It raises their price, so people buy fewer imports and more locally made goods. It also earns **revenue** for the government.

**2. Quotas.** A quota is a **limit on the quantity or value** of a good that may be imported in a given period. Once it is reached no more can enter. It protects local producers more directly than a tariff.

**3. Embargo or import licensing.** An **embargo** is a **total ban** on trade in certain goods or with a certain country (for political, health or security reasons). **Import licensing** allows imports only by firms that have obtained a permit, so the government controls what comes in.

**Other methods:** exchange controls, subsidies to local producers and administrative regulations such as strict quality standards.

**Conclusion.** These measures protect home industries and the balance of payments, but they may raise prices and lead to retaliation by trading partners.
